q: Under Canon III, Section 1 of the CPRA, the practice of law:
choices: Is the rendition of legal service or application of law and legal judgment, in or out of court, pursuant to a lawyer-client relationship or other engagement, and requires membership in the Bar
Includes any work by a law graduate
hints: It is not limited to court work.
Legal advice and drafting count.
why: CPRA Canon III, Sec. 1 defines the practice of law as rendering legal service or applying law, in or out of court, pursuant to a lawyer-client relationship or other engagement, including employment in public or private sector, requiring Bar membership; Cayetano v. Monsod, G.R. No. 100113, September 3, 1991, held that it covers any activity requiring the application of legal knowledge, training and experience.
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon III, Sec. 1; Cayetano v. Monsod, G.R. No. 100113, September 3, 1991

q: Lito, who passed the Bar but never signed the Roll of Attorneys, opened an office where he drafts contracts and gives legal advice for a fee, though he never appears in court. Is he engaged in the practice of law?

alac.answer: Yes, Lito is engaged in the practice of law, and doing so without having signed the Roll is unauthorized practice.
alac.basis: Canon III, Section 1 of the CPRA defines the practice of law as the rendition of legal service or performance of acts or the application of law, legal principles, and judgment, in or out of court, with regard to the circumstances or objectives of a person or a cause, and it requires membership in the Philippine bar. In Cayetano v. Monsod, G.R. No. 100113, September 3, 1991, the Supreme Court held that the practice of law means any activity, in or out of court, which requires the application of law, legal procedure, knowledge, training and experience.
alac.application: Here, Lito drafts contracts and gives legal advice for a fee, which applies legal knowledge to clients' situations, even though he does not appear in court. But he has not signed the Roll of Attorneys, so he is not yet a member of the Bar.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Lito is practicing law without being a member of the Bar, which is unauthorized practice and may be punished by contempt and bar his admission.

keyPoints: Practice of law defined (CPRA Canon III, Sec. 1)
Includes work out of court (Cayetano v. Monsod)
Requires membership in the Bar
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon III, Sec. 1; Cayetano v. Monsod, G.R. No. 100113, September 3, 1991

q: The practice of law is:
choices: A natural right of every law graduate
A privilege burdened with conditions, granted only to those who meet the standards and continue to meet them
A property right that cannot be taken away
A right guaranteed by the Bill of Rights
hints: Admission is not a vested right.
Continued good standing is a condition.
why: The practice of law is a privilege burdened with conditions: mental fitness, the highest degree of morality, and faithful compliance with the rules of the profession are conditions for remaining a member in good standing; the privilege may be suspended or revoked in disciplinary proceedings.
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC); Rule 138, Rules of Court

q: A lawyer suspended for misconduct argues that the Supreme Court violated his property rights because law is his means of livelihood and his license is his property. Is the argument valid?

alac.answer: No, the argument is not valid.
alac.basis: The practice of law is a privilege burdened with conditions, not a right. Adherence to rigid standards of mental fitness, maintenance of the highest degree of morality, and faithful compliance with the rules of the legal profession are the conditions required for remaining a member of good standing of the bar and for enjoying the privilege to practice law. The Supreme Court may suspend or revoke the privilege when these conditions are violated.
alac.application: Here, the lawyer was suspended for misconduct, which shows a failure to comply with the conditions of the privilege. His license is not a property right protected against such regulation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the suspension does not violate any property right.

keyPoints: Practice of law is a privilege, not a right
Conditions: fitness, morality, compliance with rules
May be suspended or revoked
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC); Rule 138, Rules of Court

q: Under Article VIII, Section 5(5) of the 1987 Constitution, the power to promulgate rules on the admission to the practice of law and the integrated bar belongs to:
hints: Congress cannot admit lawyers by law.
Discipline of lawyers is also within the Court's power.
why: Const. Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5) vests in the Supreme Court exclusive power over admission to the practice of law, the integrated bar, and legal assistance; Congress cannot pass laws that admit lawyers or set aside the Court's rules on the Bar.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5)

q: Congress passed a law declaring that all law graduates who scored at least 70% in the Bar exams of the last ten years are deemed to have passed and shall be admitted. Is the law valid?

alac.answer: No, the law is unconstitutional.
alac.basis: Article VIII, Section 5(5) of the 1987 Constitution grants the Supreme Court the power to promulgate rules concerning the admission to the practice of law and the integrated bar. The admission, supervision and discipline of lawyers are exclusively within the Supreme Court's jurisdiction; Congress cannot, by legislation, admit persons to the Bar or alter the Court's rules on admission.
alac.application: Here, the law would admit to the Bar persons who failed to meet the Court's passing standards, which encroaches on the Court's exclusive power over admission to the practice of law.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the law is void for violating the separation of powers and the Supreme Court's constitutional power.

keyPoints: Supreme Court's power over admission to the practice of law (Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5))
Exclusive; Congress cannot admit lawyers
Includes supervision and discipline
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5)

q: Before taking the Bar exams, an applicant must show that he has:
choices: Worked in a law firm for five years
Completed the prescribed pre-law and law courses for the law degree in a recognized school
Passed a government civil service exam
hints: Pre-law and law degree requirements must be met.
Fraud in qualifications voids admission.
why: Rule 138, Sec. 5 (as amended) requires completion of the prescribed law courses in a duly recognized law school, and the pre-law requirements; RA 7662 created the Legal Education Board to regulate legal education. A person who did not finish the required education cannot be admitted (Caronan v. Caronan, A.C. No. 11316, July 12, 2016).
cite: Rule 138, Sec. 5, Rules of Court; Legal Education Reform Act (RA 7662)

q: Pat used his brother's college records to enroll in law school, graduated, passed the Bar, and practiced for years, though he never finished college himself. When discovered, he argued that passing the Bar cures any defect. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, Pat is not correct; his name should be stricken from the Roll of Attorneys.
alac.basis: Rule 138 of the Rules of Court requires applicants for admission to the Bar to show that they have successfully completed the prescribed pre-law and law courses. In Caronan v. Caronan, A.C. No. 11316, July 12, 2016, the Supreme Court ordered the name of a lawyer who used his brother's identity and records, without having finished college, stricken from the Roll of Attorneys, and barred him from admission, because he never met the educational requirements.
alac.application: Here, Pat never completed college, a prerequisite for law school and Bar admission, and used another person's records. Passing the Bar does not cure the absence of the required qualifications or the fraud.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Pat's admission is void, his name should be stricken from the Roll, and he may face criminal and other liabilities.

keyPoints: Educational requirements for the Bar (Rule 138)
Fraud in qualifications voids admission (Caronan v. Caronan)
Passing the Bar does not cure lack of qualifications
cite: Rule 138, Sec. 5, Rules of Court; Legal Education Reform Act (RA 7662)

q: Under Rule 138 of the Rules of Court, an applicant for admission to the Bar must be:
choices: Any foreigner with a law degree
hints: Loss of citizenship terminates the privilege to practice.
Reacquisition under RA 9225 requires Court approval to resume practice.
why: Rule 138, Sec. 2 requires that applicants be Filipino citizens (with good moral character and the other requirements); a lawyer who loses Filipino citizenship loses the privilege to practice, but may resume it upon reacquiring citizenship under RA 9225 and complying with the Court's conditions.
cite: Rule 138, Sec. 2, Rules of Court, as amended

q: Atty. Rey became a naturalized American citizen and stopped practicing. He later reacquired Philippine citizenship under RA 9225 and wants to resume law practice immediately. May he?

alac.answer: He may resume practice only after securing the Supreme Court's permission upon compliance with its conditions.
alac.basis: Rule 138 of the Rules of Court requires that every applicant for admission as a member of the bar must be a citizen of the Philippines, and Filipino citizenship is a continuing requirement for the practice of law. A lawyer who lost Philippine citizenship loses the privilege to practice; upon reacquiring citizenship under RA 9225, he must petition the Supreme Court for leave to resume practice, and the Court may require compliance with conditions such as payment of IBP dues, professional tax, MCLE, and retaking the lawyer's oath.
alac.application: Here, Atty. Rey lost his Philippine citizenship upon naturalization and thereby lost his privilege to practice. Although he reacquired citizenship, his privilege is not automatically restored.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he must petition the Supreme Court and comply with its conditions before resuming practice.

keyPoints: Citizenship is a requirement for admission and continued practice (Rule 138)
Loss of citizenship terminates the privilege
Resumption after RA 9225 needs Supreme Court leave
cite: Rule 138, Sec. 2, Rules of Court, as amended

q: Good moral character as a requirement for the practice of law is:
choices: Required only at the time of the Bar exams
A continuing requirement, both for admission and for remaining a member of the Bar
hints: The applicant must disclose pending charges.
Misconduct after admission is also a ground for discipline.
why: Good moral character is required for admission (Rule 138, Sec. 2) and is a continuing condition of the privilege to practice; concealment of pending charges or misconduct before admission may lead to disbarment or denial of admission.
cite: Rule 138, Sec. 2, Rules of Court; Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC)

q: Bar applicant Dana did not disclose in her application a pending criminal case for estafa against her. After she passed the Bar, the concealment was discovered before her oath-taking. Should she be allowed to take the oath?

alac.answer: No, she should not be allowed to take the oath until the matter is resolved, and her concealment itself may warrant denial of admission.
alac.basis: Rule 138, Section 2 of the Rules of Court requires every applicant for admission to the Bar to be of good moral character and to produce satisfactory evidence of good moral character and that no charges involving moral turpitude have been filed or are pending. Good moral character is a continuing requirement, and candor in the application is part of it; concealing a pending case is itself a lack of good moral character.
alac.application: Here, Dana concealed a pending criminal case for estafa, a crime involving moral turpitude, in her application. This raises doubts about her moral character, both because of the charge and because of her lack of candor.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the Supreme Court may deny or defer her admission until the case is resolved and may consider her concealment in deciding whether she is fit to be admitted.

keyPoints: Good moral character required for admission (Rule 138, Sec. 2)
Duty to disclose pending charges
Concealment shows lack of candor and good moral character
cite: Rule 138, Sec. 2, Rules of Court; Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC)

q: The Bar examinations are administered under the authority of:
choices: The Supreme Court, through the Bar Examination Committee chaired by a Justice
hints: Bar Bulletins govern each Bar.
The 2027 Bar uses essay problems answered in ALAC form.
why: The Supreme Court conducts the Bar examinations under its power over admission (Const. Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5)); the Bar Chairperson (a Justice) issues Bar Bulletins on coverage and procedures. For 2027, the exam is digital and regional, with 20 essay problems per subject.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5); Rule 138, Rules of Court; 2027 Bar Bulletins

q: A Bar examinee asked a court to order the Supreme Court to recheck his Bar exam answers, claiming his grade was wrong. Does the court have jurisdiction?

alac.answer: No; the conduct and grading of the Bar examinations are within the Supreme Court's exclusive power, and no lower court may review them.
alac.basis: Article VIII, Section 5(5) of the 1987 Constitution gives the Supreme Court the power to promulgate rules concerning the admission to the practice of law. The Bar examinations are conducted by the Supreme Court, through the Bar Examination Committee, as part of that power; the grading and the release of results are within its exclusive authority, and lower courts cannot review or control them.
alac.application: Here, the examinee seeks to compel the Supreme Court, through a lower court, to recheck his answers. The lower court has no authority over the Supreme Court's admission processes.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the case must be dismissed; the examinee may only seek relief from the Supreme Court itself, under its rules.

keyPoints: Bar examinations under the Supreme Court's power over admission
Grading within the Court's exclusive authority
Lower courts have no jurisdiction
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5); Rule 138, Rules of Court; 2027 Bar Bulletins

q: The Revised Lawyer's Oath adopted with the CPRA in 2023 is significant because:
choices: It is the lawyer's solemn undertaking to uphold the Constitution and laws and to act with honesty and fidelity, and its violation is a ground for discipline
It applies only to government lawyers
hints: The oath is taken before signing the Roll.
Breach of the oath is a disciplinary offense.
why: Taking the lawyer's oath is a requirement for admission (Rule 138); the CPRA adopted a revised oath; violating the oath is a ground for disciplinary action under the CPRA.
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC) (Revised Lawyer's Oath)

q: A newly admitted lawyer posted online that he intends to "bend any law" to win his clients' cases. A complaint was filed against him for violating his oath. Is the complaint proper?

alac.answer: Yes, the complaint is proper; he may be disciplined for conduct contrary to his oath.
alac.basis: Every lawyer, upon admission, takes the lawyer's oath, now the Revised Lawyer's Oath adopted with the CPRA, by which he solemnly undertakes to uphold the Constitution, obey the laws and legal orders, do no falsehood, and conduct himself with fidelity to the courts and his clients within the bounds of law. A lawyer who violates the lawyer's oath and transgresses the canons of the CPRA may be disciplined.
alac.application: Here, the lawyer publicly declared that he would bend the law to win cases, which contradicts his sworn undertaking to obey the laws and act within their bounds, and undermines public confidence in the profession.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he may be disciplined for violating his oath and the CPRA, the penalty depending on the circumstances.

keyPoints: Lawyer's oath as a condition of admission
Revised Lawyer's Oath with the CPRA
Violation of the oath is a ground for discipline
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC) (Revised Lawyer's Oath)

q: A person who passed the Bar and took the oath but has not signed the Roll of Attorneys:
choices: Is not yet a member of the Bar and may not practice law
May practice in lower courts only
hints: Admission is completed by signing the Roll.
Practicing before signing is unauthorized practice.
why: Signing the Roll of Attorneys is the last act that completes admission to the Bar; until then, a person is not a lawyer and cannot practice. Striking a name from the Roll ends the person's status as a lawyer.
cite: Rule 138, Rules of Court; Caronan v. Caronan, A.C. No. 11316, July 12, 2016

q: Ivy passed the Bar and took her oath, but before signing the Roll of Attorneys she appeared as counsel in a hearing and signed a pleading. What is her status, and what are the consequences?

alac.answer: Ivy is not yet a lawyer; her appearance and signing a pleading are unauthorized practice of law.
alac.basis: Under Rule 138 of the Rules of Court, admission to the Bar is completed only upon signing the Roll of Attorneys after taking the oath. A person who has passed the Bar and taken the oath but has not signed the Roll is not yet a member of the Bar and may not practice law. The Supreme Court has sanctioned such persons by delaying or denying their signing of the Roll.
alac.application: Here, Ivy appeared as counsel and signed a pleading before signing the Roll, so she practiced law without being a member of the Bar.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she engaged in unauthorized practice of law and may be held in contempt and have her signing of the Roll delayed.

keyPoints: Signing the Roll of Attorneys completes admission
No practice before signing
Sanctions for premature practice
cite: Rule 138, Rules of Court; Caronan v. Caronan, A.C. No. 11316, July 12, 2016

q: Under Bar Matter No. 850, the purpose of Mandatory Continuing Legal Education is to:
choices: Ensure that lawyers keep abreast with law and jurisprudence, maintain the ethics of the profession and enhance the standards of practice
hints: Some officials and groups are exempt.
Non-compliance results in delinquency.
why: BM 850 requires IBP members to complete MCLE units in each compliance period; non-compliant lawyers are listed as delinquent and may not practice until compliance, and pleadings must state MCLE compliance details. Violation of Supreme Court rules on Bar matters is a less serious offense under CPRA Canon VI, Sec. 34(c).
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon VI, Sec. 34(c); Bar Matter No. 850 (MCLE), as amended

q: Atty. Joy failed to complete her MCLE units for the last compliance period and was declared delinquent. She continued filing pleadings in court. What are the consequences?

alac.answer: She may be disciplined, and her practice while delinquent is unauthorized.
alac.basis: Bar Matter No. 850 requires members of the IBP to undergo Mandatory Continuing Legal Education to ensure that lawyers keep abreast with law and jurisprudence, maintain the ethics of the profession, and enhance the standards of practice. A member who fails to comply is listed as a delinquent member and may not practice until compliance. Under Canon VI, Section 34(c) of the CPRA, violation of Supreme Court rules and issuances in relation to Bar matters is a less serious offense.
alac.application: Here, Atty. Joy was declared delinquent for MCLE non-compliance but continued to file pleadings, practicing while delinquent.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she may be disciplined under the CPRA, and she must complete her MCLE units before practicing again.

keyPoints: MCLE purpose (BM 850)
Delinquency for non-compliance
Violation of Bar rules is a less serious offense (CPRA Canon VI, Sec. 34(c))
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon VI, Sec. 34(c); Bar Matter No. 850 (MCLE), as amended

q: Under the rules on the Integrated Bar, a lawyer's failure to pay IBP membership dues for a long period may result in:
choices: Suspension of membership and, in proper cases, removal of the name from the Roll of Attorneys
hints: Integration of the Bar is valid.
Dues are a regulatory requirement.
why: Membership in the IBP is mandatory, and payment of dues is a condition of continued membership; prolonged default may lead to suspension and removal from the Roll. Compulsory dues do not violate freedom of association.
cite: Rule 139-A (Integrated Bar), Rules of Court; Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC)

q: A lawyer refused to pay IBP dues, arguing that compulsory membership and dues violate his freedom of association. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, he is not correct.
alac.basis: The integration of the Philippine Bar was made by the Supreme Court under its constitutional power over the integrated bar, and payment of membership dues is a condition for remaining a member in good standing. Compulsory membership in the IBP and payment of dues are valid regulatory measures that do not violate freedom of association, since the lawyer is not compelled to join any political or other association, only to bear his share in regulating the profession he chose.
alac.application: Here, the lawyer refused to pay his dues. Membership in the IBP is a condition of his privilege to practice, and the dues support the regulation of the profession.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, his refusal is not justified, and he may be suspended and eventually removed from the Roll for continued non-payment.

keyPoints: Integrated Bar membership compulsory
Dues as a condition of good standing
No violation of freedom of association
cite: Rule 139-A (Integrated Bar), Rules of Court; Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC)

q: Under Section 139 of the Local Government Code, a lawyer pays professional tax:
choices: To every city where he appears
To the province (or city) where he practices or maintains his principal office if he practices in several places
hints: The PTR number appears in pleadings.
One payment covers practice nationwide.
why: LGC Sec. 139: lawyers pay an annual professional tax to the province (or city) where they practice or have their principal office; payment entitles them to practice anywhere in the Philippines; the PTR number must be indicated in pleadings.
cite: Local Government Code (RA 7160), Sec. 139

q: A lawyer whose principal office is in Makati appeared in a court in Iloilo. The Iloilo court refused to accept his pleading because he had no Iloilo professional tax receipt. Is the court correct?

alac.answer: No, the court is not correct.
alac.basis: Section 139 of the Local Government Code provides that every person legally authorized to practice his profession shall pay the professional tax to the province where he practices or where he maintains his principal office in case he practices in several places, and that a person who has paid the corresponding professional tax shall be entitled to practice his profession in any part of the Philippines without being subjected to any other national or local tax, license, or fee for its practice.
alac.application: Here, the lawyer maintains his principal office in Makati and presumably paid his professional tax there. That payment entitles him to practice anywhere, including Iloilo.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should accept his pleading, provided it indicates his PTR details.

keyPoints: Professional tax paid where the principal office is (LGC Sec. 139)
Payment entitles practice anywhere in the Philippines
PTR stated in pleadings
cite: Local Government Code (RA 7160), Sec. 139

q: Under the Unified Legal Aid Service (ULAS) rules (AM 22-11-01-SC):
choices: Legal aid is purely voluntary for all lawyers
Practicing lawyers must render a minimum number of hours of free legal aid service within each compliance period, as a continuing requirement
Only PAO lawyers give legal aid
Legal aid is done only by law students
hints: ULAS sets a minimum number of hours.
Non-compliance has consequences similar to MCLE.
why: AM 22-11-01-SC requires practicing lawyers to render free legal aid services for a minimum number of hours in each compliance period, reported to the IBP/Supreme Court; the PAO is the government's primary legal aid office (CPRA Canon III, Sec. 22), and the CPRA treats legal aid as a duty of fidelity to the cause of justice.
cite: Unified Legal Aid Service Rules (AM 22-11-01-SC); Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon III, Sec. 22

q: A busy corporate lawyer argued that he is exempt from rendering free legal aid because he does not do litigation and his firm pays high taxes. Is he exempt under the ULAS rules?

alac.answer: No, he is not exempt merely because he does not litigate or because his firm pays taxes.
alac.basis: The Unified Legal Aid Service Rules (AM 22-11-01-SC) require practicing lawyers to render a minimum number of hours of free legal aid services within each compliance period, unless they fall within the specific exemptions provided by the Rules. The CPRA likewise treats access to legal services as part of a lawyer's duty of fidelity to the cause of justice, and recognizes the Public Attorney's Office as the primary legal aid service office of the government.
alac.application: Here, the lawyer is a practicing lawyer. Being a corporate lawyer or paying taxes is not among the grounds for exemption; legal aid may include non-litigation services such as legal advice and documentation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he must comply with the ULAS requirement or face the consequences for non-compliance.

keyPoints: ULAS minimum legal aid hours (AM 22-11-01-SC)
Applies to practicing lawyers unless exempt
Legal aid as part of the duty of fidelity
cite: Unified Legal Aid Service Rules (AM 22-11-01-SC); Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon III, Sec. 22

q: Under Article VI, Section 14 of the Constitution, a Senator who is a lawyer:
choices: May not practice law at all
May practice law but may not personally appear as counsel before any court, the Electoral Tribunals, or quasi-judicial and other administrative bodies
hints: The ban is on personal appearance.
Office practice is not prohibited.
why: Const. Art. VI, Sec. 14 does not bar members of Congress from the practice of law, but prohibits them from personally appearing as counsel before courts, Electoral Tribunals, and quasi-judicial and administrative bodies; they may still give advice and prepare documents.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 14

q: Senator Ana, a lawyer, drafted a contract for a friend's company and also filed her appearance as counsel for the company in a case before the NLRC. Which acts are allowed?

alac.answer: Drafting the contract is allowed, but appearing as counsel before the NLRC is not.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 14 of the 1987 Constitution provides that no Senator or Member of the House of Representatives may personally appear as counsel before any court of justice or before the Electoral Tribunals, or quasi-judicial and other administrative bodies. The prohibition is limited to personal appearance; it does not bar other forms of law practice.
alac.application: Here, drafting a contract is law practice without appearance before a tribunal, which is allowed. The NLRC is a quasi-judicial body, so her personal appearance as counsel there is prohibited.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Senator Ana may draft the contract but must withdraw her appearance before the NLRC.

keyPoints: Members of Congress may not personally appear as counsel (Art. VI, Sec. 14)
Covers courts, Electoral Tribunals, quasi-judicial and administrative bodies
Other law practice not prohibited
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 14

q: Under Section 90(b) of the Local Government Code, a sanggunian member who is a lawyer may NOT:
choices: Appear as counsel in any civil case where a local government unit or any government office is the adverse party
Give legal advice to private clients
hints: They may practice outside session hours.
Restrictions protect the government's interests.
why: LGC Sec. 90(b): sanggunian members may practice their profession except during session hours, but lawyer-members may not appear in civil cases against government, in criminal cases against public officers for acts in office, collect fees for appearance in administrative proceedings involving their LGU, or use government property in practice.
cite: Local Government Code (RA 7160), Sec. 90(b)

q: Councilor Ben, a lawyer, was hired by a private company to sue the city government for damages. He wants to appear as the company's counsel. May he?

alac.answer: No, Councilor Ben may not appear as counsel against the city.
alac.basis: Section 90(b) of the Local Government Code provides that sanggunian members may practice their professions except during session hours, provided that sanggunian members who are also members of the Bar shall not appear as counsel before any court in any civil case wherein a local government unit or any office, agency, or instrumentality of the government is the adverse party.
alac.application: Here, Councilor Ben is a sanggunian member and a lawyer, and the civil case he would handle is against the city, a local government unit.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he is prohibited from appearing as counsel in that case.

keyPoints: Sanggunian members may practice except during session hours (Sec. 90(b))
May not appear in civil cases against government
Other listed restrictions
cite: Local Government Code (RA 7160), Sec. 90(b)

q: Under RA 910, as amended by RA 9946, a retired justice or judge receiving a pension:
choices: May not practice law at all
May practice law, but may not appear as counsel in cases against the government or in cases involving acts of public officers in the performance of their duties
May appear only before the Supreme Court
hints: The restriction protects the government.
Violation affects retirement benefits.
why: RA 910, as amended, allows retired justices and judges to practice law, subject to the condition that they shall not appear or act as counsel in civil cases in which the government is the adverse party, or in criminal cases where public officers are accused of offenses committed in the discharge of their duties; violation may result in loss of pension benefits.
cite: RA 910, as amended by RA 9946

q: Retired Judge Cruz, receiving a pension under RA 910, accepted a case defending a mayor charged with graft for acts done in office. Is this allowed?

alac.answer: No, Judge Cruz may not act as counsel in that case.
alac.basis: RA 910, as amended by RA 9946, provides that a retired justice or judge receiving a pension under it shall not appear as counsel before any court in any civil case wherein the government or any subdivision or instrumentality thereof is the adverse party, or in any criminal case wherein an officer or employee of the government is accused of an offense committed in relation to his office, nor collect fees for such appearance.
alac.application: Here, the mayor is a public officer accused of graft for acts done in office, an offense committed in relation to his office.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Judge Cruz may not act as the mayor's counsel without violating RA 910, as amended.

keyPoints: Retired justices and judges may practice law
Restriction in cases against the government or public officers' official acts
RA 910, as amended by RA 9946
cite: RA 910, as amended by RA 9946

q: Under RA 6713, a government employee who is a lawyer may engage in private practice:
choices: Only if authorized by the Constitution or law, and if it will not conflict with official functions (with written permission of the head of agency under civil service rules)
hints: Permission must be in writing.
Practice must not use office time or resources.
why: RA 6713 Sec. 7(b)(2): public officials and employees may not engage in private practice unless authorized by the Constitution or law and without conflict with their functions; civil service rules require written permission from the head of agency for practice outside office hours that does not conflict with duties.
cite: Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards (RA 6713), Sec. 7(b)(2); CSC Resolution No. 2500358

q: Atty. Dela Peña, a lawyer at the Department of Agriculture, handled private cases during office hours without his secretary's permission or the head of agency's approval. What is his liability?

alac.answer: He violated RA 6713 and civil service rules and may be held administratively liable.
alac.basis: Section 7(b)(2) of RA 6713 prohibits public officials and employees from engaging in the private practice of their profession unless authorized by the Constitution or law, provided that such practice will not conflict or tend to conflict with their official functions. Under civil service rules, such practice requires written permission from the head of agency and must be done outside office hours.
alac.application: Here, Atty. Dela Peña practiced privately during office hours and without any permission from the head of agency.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he may be administratively disciplined and may also face disciplinary action as a lawyer.

keyPoints: Prohibition on private practice of government employees (RA 6713, Sec. 7(b)(2))
Exception: authorized, non-conflicting practice
Written permission of head of agency; outside office hours
cite: Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards (RA 6713), Sec. 7(b)(2); CSC Resolution No. 2500358

q: Under RA 6713, after separation from public office, a former official who is a lawyer:
choices: May practice, but may not practice in connection with any matter before the office he used to be with for one year
hints: The ban is limited to matters before the former office.
The period is one year.
why: RA 6713 Sec. 7(b), last paragraph: for one year after separation, a former official cannot practice his profession in connection with any matter before the office he used to be with.
cite: Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards (RA 6713), Sec. 7(b), last paragraph

q: Atty. Rita resigned from the BIR in January. In June, she filed a protest before the BIR on behalf of a private taxpayer. Is this allowed?

alac.answer: No, it is not allowed until one year after her resignation.
alac.basis: The last paragraph of Section 7(b) of RA 6713 provides that the professional concerned cannot practice his profession in connection with any matter before the office he used to be with, for a period of one year after resignation, retirement, or separation from public office.
alac.application: Here, Atty. Rita filed a protest before the BIR, her former office, only five months after her resignation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she violated the one-year prohibition and may be held liable; she may handle matters before other offices.

keyPoints: One-year prohibition after separation (RA 6713, Sec. 7(b))
Limited to matters before the former office
Practice elsewhere allowed
cite: Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards (RA 6713), Sec. 7(b), last paragraph

q: Under the Revised Law Student Practice Rule (Rule 138-A, as amended by AM 19-03-24-SC), a law student practitioner may appear in court:
choices: Only if certified, enrolled in a clinical legal education program, and under the direct supervision of a supervising lawyer
hints: Certification levels depend on completed courses.
The supervising lawyer is responsible.
why: Rule 138-A, as amended by AM 19-03-24-SC, allows certified law student practitioners (Level 1 and Level 2 certification, depending on completed law courses) enrolled in a clinical legal education program to render limited legal services and, for Level 2, appear in courts under the direct supervision of a supervising lawyer; pleadings must be signed by the supervising lawyer.
cite: Rule 138-A, Rules of Court, as amended by AM 19-03-24-SC (Revised Law Student Practice Rule)

q: A third-year law student enrolled in her school's legal aid clinic, with the required Level 2 certification, wants to appear at a hearing in an RTC for an indigent client, without her supervising lawyer present. May she?

alac.answer: No, she may appear only under the direct supervision of her supervising lawyer.
alac.basis: Rule 138-A of the Rules of Court, as amended by the Revised Law Student Practice Rule (AM 19-03-24-SC), allows a certified law student practitioner enrolled in a clinical legal education program to appear in court on behalf of indigent clients, but only under the direct supervision and control of a supervising lawyer, who must sign the pleadings and is responsible for the student's conduct.
alac.application: Here, the student has the proper certification and is enrolled in a legal aid clinic, but she intends to appear without her supervising lawyer.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she may appear only if her supervising lawyer is present and supervising, as required by the Rule.

keyPoints: Law student practice (Rule 138-A, as amended)
Certification and clinical program required
Direct supervision by a supervising lawyer
cite: Rule 138-A, Rules of Court, as amended by AM 19-03-24-SC (Revised Law Student Practice Rule)

q: Under Section 37 of PD 1529, a claimant in cadastral proceedings may appear:
choices: By himself or by some other authorized person in his behalf
hints: The representative need not be a lawyer.
This is one of the exceptions to the rule.
why: PD 1529 Sec. 37 allows cadastral claimants to appear by themselves or through any authorized person, an exception to the rule that only lawyers may represent others in court.
cite: Property Registration Decree (PD 1529), Sec. 37

q: In a cadastral case, Lola Inez, an elderly claimant, authorized her non-lawyer nephew to appear and file her answer. The opposing party says only a lawyer may do so. Who is right?

alac.answer: Lola Inez is right; her nephew may appear for her.
alac.basis: Section 37 of PD 1529 provides that any claimant in cadastral proceedings shall appear before the court by himself or by some other authorized person in his behalf, and shall file an answer. This is one of the recognized instances where a non-lawyer may represent another in court.
alac.application: Here, Lola Inez authorized her nephew to appear and file her answer in the cadastral case.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the nephew may validly appear for her, although he may not charge fees as a lawyer would.

keyPoints: Cadastral claimants may appear personally or through authorized persons (PD 1529, Sec. 37)
Representative need not be a lawyer
Exception to the rule on appearance
cite: Property Registration Decree (PD 1529), Sec. 37

q: Under Article 228 (formerly 222) of the Labor Code, a non-lawyer may appear before the NLRC or a Labor Arbiter only:
choices: For any client for a fee
If he represents himself, or his organization or its members
If he is a law graduate
hints: Union officers may represent members.
Non-lawyers cannot represent outside clients for a fee.
why: Labor Code Art. 228 (renumbered from 222): non-lawyers may appear before the NLRC or Labor Arbiters only to represent themselves or their organization or its members; the DOLE rules also allow duly accredited legal aid of the DOLE.
cite: Labor Code, Art. 228 (formerly Art. 222)

q: Cesar, a non-lawyer labor consultant, represents several unrelated workers before a Labor Arbiter for a 20% fee of any award. Is this allowed?

alac.answer: No, Cesar may not represent the workers.
alac.basis: Article 228 (formerly 222) of the Labor Code provides that non-lawyers may appear before the Commission or any Labor Arbiter only if they represent themselves, or if they represent their organization or members thereof. Representing others for a fee outside these situations is unauthorized practice of law.
alac.application: Here, Cesar is not a lawyer, and he represents workers who are not members of any organization he belongs to, for a fee.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, his appearance is not allowed and may be treated as unauthorized practice of law.

keyPoints: Non-lawyer appearance before NLRC limited (Art. 228)
Only self-representation or for their organization or members
Representation of others for a fee is unauthorized practice
cite: Labor Code, Art. 228 (formerly Art. 222)

q: Under Section 50 of RA 6657, in proceedings before the DAR:
choices: Responsible farmer leaders may represent themselves, their fellow farmers, or their organizations
Only the DAR Secretary may appear
hints: This applies before the DAR, not regular courts.
Only one representative per party or group.
why: RA 6657 Sec. 50 allows responsible farmer leaders, though not lawyers, to represent themselves, fellow farmers or their organizations before the DAR; where there are several representatives, only one may be chosen to represent a party or group.
cite: Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law (RA 6657), Sec. 50, as amended by RA 9700

q: In a DAR case on land coverage, two farmer leaders, both non-lawyers, want to appear together for the same group of farmers. May they?

alac.answer: They may represent the farmers, but they must choose only one of them to represent the group.
alac.basis: Section 50 of RA 6657 provides that responsible farmer leaders shall be allowed to represent themselves, their fellow farmers, or their organizations in any proceedings before the DAR, provided that when there are two or more representatives for any individual or group, the representatives should choose only one among themselves to represent such party or group.
alac.application: Here, both farmer leaders may lawfully represent the farmers before the DAR, but since they represent the same group, only one should act as representative.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, they must choose one of them to represent the group.

keyPoints: Farmer leaders may represent before the DAR (RA 6657, Sec. 50)
Need not be lawyers
Only one representative per party or group
cite: Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law (RA 6657), Sec. 50, as amended by RA 9700

q: Under Section 415 of the Local Government Code, in katarungang pambarangay proceedings:
choices: Parties must be represented by lawyers
Parties must appear in person without counsel or representative, except minors and incompetents, who may be assisted by non-lawyer next-of-kin
hints: Lawyers are excluded to encourage settlement.
Even a lawyer-party appears as a party, not as counsel.
why: LGC Sec. 415 requires personal appearance in barangay conciliation, without lawyers or representatives, to encourage amicable settlement; minors and incompetents may be assisted by next-of-kin who are not lawyers.
cite: Local Government Code (RA 7160), Sec. 415

q: In a barangay conciliation for a debt, the creditor sent his lawyer to appear for him. The debtor, a 16-year-old, came with his father, who is not a lawyer. Are these appearances allowed?

alac.answer: The lawyer's appearance for the creditor is not allowed, but the father may assist the minor debtor.
alac.basis: Section 415 of the Local Government Code provides that in all katarungang pambarangay proceedings, the parties must appear in person without the assistance of counsel or representative, except for minors and incompetents who may be assisted by their next-of-kin who are not lawyers.
alac.application: Here, the creditor did not appear personally but sent his lawyer, which the law prohibits. The debtor is a minor, and his father, a non-lawyer next-of-kin, may assist him.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the creditor must appear personally, while the minor may be assisted by his father.

keyPoints: Personal appearance required (LGC Sec. 415)
No counsel or representative
Exception: minors and incompetents with non-lawyer next-of-kin
cite: Local Government Code (RA 7160), Sec. 415

q: In small claims cases under the Rules on Expedited Procedures, as a rule:
choices: No attorney shall appear on behalf of a party at the hearing unless the attorney is himself the plaintiff or defendant
hints: The procedure is designed to be simple and lawyer-free.
Juridical persons appear through authorized representatives.
why: Under the small claims rules (AM 08-8-7-SC, as amended, Rule IV, Secs. 17-18), parties appear personally; no attorney may appear for a party unless the attorney is the party; juridical entities appear through authorized non-lawyer representatives; a party who cannot properly present his claim may be assisted by a non-lawyer with the court's permission.
cite: Rules on Expedited Procedures in the First Level Courts (AM 08-8-7-SC, as amended), Rule IV, Secs. 17-18

q: In a small claims case, a corporation sent its in-house lawyer to appear and argue at the hearing as its representative. Is this allowed?

alac.answer: No; the corporation must appear through an authorized representative who is not acting as its lawyer.
alac.basis: Under Rule IV, Sections 17 and 18 of the Rules on Expedited Procedures in the First Level Courts (AM 08-8-7-SC, as amended), no attorney shall appear in behalf of or represent a party at the hearing of a small claims case, unless the attorney is the plaintiff or defendant; juridical entities shall appear through an authorized representative, who must not be a lawyer acting as counsel.
alac.application: Here, the corporation sent its in-house lawyer to appear and argue at the hearing, which is appearance by an attorney on behalf of a party.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the corporation should send a duly authorized non-lawyer representative instead.

keyPoints: No lawyers in small claims hearings (AM 08-8-7-SC, Rule IV)
Exception: the lawyer is the party
Juridical entities appear through authorized representatives
cite: Rules on Expedited Procedures in the First Level Courts (AM 08-8-7-SC, as amended), Rule IV, Secs. 17-18

q: Under Section 22 of RA 9285, in international arbitration conducted in the Philippines, a party may be represented by:
choices: Any person of his choice, though a representative not admitted to the Philippine Bar may not appear as counsel in Philippine courts
hints: Foreign lawyers may appear in arbitration.
They cannot appear in Philippine courts.
why: RA 9285 Sec. 22: parties in international arbitration in the Philippines may be represented by any person of their choice, including foreign lawyers, but such representatives, unless admitted here, may not appear in Philippine courts or quasi-judicial bodies; Sec. 33 extends this to domestic arbitration.
cite: Alternative Dispute Resolution Act (RA 9285), Secs. 22 and 33

q: A Singaporean lawyer represented a foreign company in an international arbitration held in Manila. Later, he filed a petition in the RTC to confirm the arbitral award, signing as counsel. Are his acts allowed?

alac.answer: His representation in the arbitration is allowed, but he may not appear as counsel in the RTC.
alac.basis: Section 22 of RA 9285 provides that in international arbitration conducted in the Philippines, a party may be presented by any person of his choice, provided that such representative, unless admitted to the practice of law in the Philippines, shall not be authorized to appear as counsel in any Philippine court, or any other quasi-judicial body, whether or not such appearance is in relation to the arbitration in which he appears.
alac.application: Here, the Singaporean lawyer's representation in the international arbitration is permitted. But the petition to confirm the award is filed in a Philippine court, where he is not authorized to appear as counsel.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the company must engage a Philippine lawyer for the RTC proceedings.

keyPoints: Representation by any person in international arbitration (RA 9285, Sec. 22)
No appearance in Philippine courts unless admitted here
Applies even if related to the arbitration
cite: Alternative Dispute Resolution Act (RA 9285), Secs. 22 and 33

q: Under Article VII, Section 13 of the Constitution, the President, Vice-President, Cabinet members, and their deputies or assistants:
choices: Shall not, during their tenure, directly or indirectly practice any other profession
May practice only in the Supreme Court
hints: The prohibition is absolute during tenure.
It covers deputies and assistants.
why: Const. Art. VII, Sec. 13 absolutely bars the President, Vice-President, Cabinet members and their deputies or assistants from practicing any other profession during their tenure.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. VII, Sec. 13

q: An Undersecretary of Justice, a lawyer, continued to give paid legal opinions to a private corporation on weekends. Is this allowed?

alac.answer: No, it is prohibited.
alac.basis: Article VII, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the President, Vice-President, the Members of the Cabinet, and their deputies or assistants shall not, during their tenure, directly or indirectly, practice any other profession. An Undersecretary is a deputy or assistant of a Cabinet member.
alac.application: Here, the Undersecretary gives paid legal opinions, which is the practice of law, during his tenure. Doing so on weekends does not matter, since the prohibition is absolute.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he violates the Constitution and may face administrative and disciplinary sanctions.

keyPoints: Absolute prohibition on practice (Art. VII, Sec. 13)
Covers Cabinet members' deputies and assistants
During the entire tenure
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. VII, Sec. 13

q: Under Article IX-A, Section 2 of the Constitution, members of the Constitutional Commissions:
choices: Shall not, during their tenure, engage in the practice of any profession
May practice only in election cases
hints: Covers CSC, COMELEC and COA.
The ban applies during tenure.
why: Const. Art. IX-A, Sec. 2: members of the CSC, COMELEC and COA may not hold other office, practice any profession, manage businesses affected by their office, or have financial interest in government contracts during their tenure.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. IX-A, Sec. 2

q: A COMELEC Commissioner, a lawyer, agreed to represent his cousin in a land dispute in the RTC, without fee. Is this allowed?

alac.answer: No, it is not allowed.
alac.basis: Article IX-A, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution provides that no member of a Constitutional Commission shall, during his tenure, hold any other office or employment, or engage in the practice of any profession.
alac.application: Here, the COMELEC Commissioner would represent his cousin in court, which is the practice of law, during his tenure. That he charges no fee does not matter.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the Commissioner is prohibited from representing his cousin.

keyPoints: Prohibition on members of Constitutional Commissions (Art. IX-A, Sec. 2)
No practice of any profession during tenure
Even without fee
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. IX-A, Sec. 2

q: Under Article XI, Section 8 of the Constitution, the Ombudsman and his Deputies during their tenure:
choices: Are subject to the same disqualifications and prohibitions as members of the Constitutional Commissions, including the ban on practice of any profession
May practice only in the Sandiganbayan
Are not covered by any prohibition
hints: The Ombudsman must be a lawyer.
But he may not practice during tenure.
why: Const. Art. XI, Sec. 8 applies to the Ombudsman and Deputies the prohibitions of Art. IX-A, Sec. 2, including the ban on practicing any profession during their tenure.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XI, Sec. 8

q: A Deputy Ombudsman, on leave for a month, wants to handle a private arbitration for a friend's company for a fee. May he?

alac.answer: No; he remains prohibited from practicing law during his tenure, even while on leave.
alac.basis: Article XI, Section 8 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the Ombudsman and his Deputies, during their tenure, shall be subject to the same disqualifications and prohibitions as provided for in Section 2 of Article IX-A, which bars engaging in the practice of any profession.
alac.application: Here, the Deputy Ombudsman is still in office, though on leave, so he is within his tenure. Handling an arbitration for a company for a fee is the practice of law.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he may not take the case.

keyPoints: Ombudsman and Deputies subject to Art. IX-A, Sec. 2 prohibitions (Art. XI, Sec. 8)
No practice during tenure
Leave does not end tenure
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XI, Sec. 8

q: Justices, judges and court employees, during their service:
choices: Are prohibited from engaging in the private practice of law
hints: The prohibition applies during service.
Post-service restrictions also apply.
why: Under the 2025 CJCA (Canon IV) and the Code of Conduct for court personnel, justices, judges and court employees may not engage in private practice of law; after separation, the CPRA restricts practice on matters before their former office for one year, and bars them from appearing in courts where they previously served for a period.
cite: 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (CJCA, AM 25-04-04-SC), Canon IV, Secs. 16 and 19; 2025 Code of Conduct and Accountability for Court Officials and Personnel (AM 25-06-11-SC)

q: A court stenographer who is a lawyer prepared and notarized deeds for private clients for a fee during her free time. Is this allowed?

alac.answer: No; as a court employee she may not engage in the private practice of law.
alac.basis: Under the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability and the 2025 Code of Conduct and Accountability for Court Officials and Personnel, justices, judges, and court officials and employees are prohibited from engaging in the private practice of law, because their duties require full time and the practice may create conflicts and erode public confidence in the judiciary. After separation, the CPRA also restricts former court personnel from engaging in private practice on any matter before the office where they used to be connected within one year.
alac.application: Here, the stenographer, a court employee, prepared and notarized deeds for paying clients, which is the private practice of law.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she violated the prohibition and may be disciplined both as a court employee and as a lawyer.

keyPoints: Court personnel may not engage in private practice
CJCA and the Code of Conduct for court personnel (2025)
One-year post-service restriction (CPRA)
cite: 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (CJCA, AM 25-04-04-SC), Canon IV, Secs. 16 and 19; 2025 Code of Conduct and Accountability for Court Officials and Personnel (AM 25-06-11-SC)

q: Under Section 90(a) of the Local Government Code, governors and mayors who are lawyers:
choices: Are prohibited from practicing their profession
May practice only in their province
May practice if no fees are charged
hints: Contrast with sanggunian members, who may practice.
The ban is absolute.
why: LGC Sec. 90(a) absolutely prohibits governors and city and municipal mayors from practicing their profession or any other occupation besides their functions as local chief executives.
cite: Local Government Code (RA 7160), Sec. 90(a)

q: Mayor Gil, a lawyer, continued to appear as counsel in a few long-time private cases after he assumed office, claiming he would do so only after office hours. Is this allowed?

alac.answer: No, it is not allowed.
alac.basis: Section 90(a) of the Local Government Code provides that all governors, city and municipal mayors are prohibited from practicing their profession or engaging in any occupation other than the exercise of their functions as local chief executives.
alac.application: Here, Mayor Gil continued to appear as counsel in private cases, which is the practice of law, while serving as mayor. That he would do so only after office hours does not matter.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he must withdraw from the cases.

keyPoints: Absolute prohibition for governors and mayors (LGC Sec. 90(a))
No practice of profession
Contrast with sanggunian members
cite: Local Government Code (RA 7160), Sec. 90(a)

q: Under Section 7(b)(2) of RA 6713, other government officials and employees may engage in the private practice of their profession:
choices: Only if authorized by the Constitution or law and if the practice will not conflict with their official functions
hints: Authorization must come from the Constitution or law.
No conflict with official functions.
why: RA 6713 Sec. 7(b)(2) generally bars public officials and employees from private practice unless authorized by the Constitution or law and without conflict with official functions; violation is punishable administratively and criminally.
cite: Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards (RA 6713), Sec. 7(b)(2)

q: A lawyer employed as legal officer of a government bank also represented private borrowers seeking loan restructuring with the same bank. Is this allowed?

alac.answer: No, it is not allowed.
alac.basis: Section 7(b)(2) of RA 6713 prohibits public officials and employees from engaging in the private practice of their profession unless authorized by the Constitution or law, provided that such practice will not conflict or tend to conflict with their official functions.
alac.application: Here, the legal officer represented private borrowers against his own employer, the government bank, in matters within his official functions. This clearly conflicts with his duties, and no law authorizes it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he violated RA 6713 and may also be disciplined under the CPRA for conflict of interest.

keyPoints: Prohibition on private practice (RA 6713, Sec. 7(b)(2))
Exception only if authorized and non-conflicting
Conflict with official functions
cite: Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards (RA 6713), Sec. 7(b)(2)

q: Under Rules 12-13 of the MCLE Rules (BM 850), a lawyer who fails to comply with MCLE:
choices: Is listed as a delinquent member and may not practice until he complies
hints: Delinquency bars practice until compliance.
Compliance details must appear in pleadings.
why: BM 850 Rule 12: non-compliant lawyers are notified and, if they fail to comply, listed as delinquent members; Rule 13: they may be reinstated upon compliance; pleadings must show MCLE compliance details, and failure to disclose may lead to dismissal of the pleading.
cite: Bar Matter No. 850 (MCLE Rules), Rules 12-13, as amended

q: A lawyer listed as MCLE-delinquent continued to sign and file pleadings, omitting his MCLE details. What are the consequences?

alac.answer: He may not practice while delinquent; his pleadings may be expunged, and he may be disciplined.
alac.basis: Under Rules 12 and 13 of the MCLE Rules (Bar Matter No. 850), a member who fails to comply with MCLE requirements after notice is listed as a delinquent member of the IBP and may not practice law until he complies and is reinstated. Pleadings must indicate the lawyer's MCLE compliance details; pleadings without them may be expunged.
alac.application: Here, the lawyer, while delinquent, continued to file pleadings and omitted his MCLE details.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, his pleadings may be expunged from the records, and he may be held liable under the CPRA for practicing while delinquent.

keyPoints: MCLE delinquency (BM 850, Rules 12-13)
No practice until compliance
Pleadings must show MCLE details
cite: Bar Matter No. 850 (MCLE Rules), Rules 12-13, as amended

q: A lawyer who practices law while under suspension:
choices: Commits unauthorized practice and may be disbarred, and may be held in contempt
hints: Suspension means no practice at all.
Resumption requires the Court's lifting of the suspension.
why: A suspended lawyer may not practice; doing so is unauthorized practice, punishable by contempt (Rule 71, Sec. 3(e)) and a ground for more severe discipline, including disbarment, under the CPRA.
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability, Canon VI

q: Atty. Mike, suspended for one year, continued to appear in court using the name of his associate on the pleadings. What is his liability?

alac.answer: He may be held in indirect contempt and disbarred or given a heavier penalty.
alac.basis: A lawyer suspended from practice may not engage in any act constituting the practice of law until the suspension is lifted. Rule 71, Section 3(e) of the Rules of Court punishes as indirect contempt assuming to be an attorney or an officer of a court, and acting as such without authority. Under the CPRA, practicing law while suspended is a serious offense that may warrant disbarment.
alac.application: Here, Atty. Mike continued to appear in court during his suspension and tried to conceal it by using his associate's name, which shows deliberate defiance of the Court's order.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he may be cited for indirect contempt and disbarred or given a heavier penalty, and his associate may also be disciplined.

keyPoints: No practice during suspension
Indirect contempt under Rule 71, Sec. 3(e)
Ground for heavier discipline or disbarment
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability, Canon VI

q: As a rule, a foreign lawyer not admitted to the Philippine Bar:
choices: May not practice law in the Philippines, except as allowed by law, such as representing parties in international arbitration
May sign pleadings with a local lawyer
hints: Citizenship is a requirement for admission.
Arbitration is an exception.
why: Only members of the Philippine Bar, who must be Filipino citizens, may practice law here; foreign lawyers may act only within exceptions such as RA 9285 Sec. 22 (international arbitration) and may not appear in Philippine courts.
cite: Rule 138, Rules of Court; Alternative Dispute Resolution Act (RA 9285), Sec. 22

q: An American lawyer working in a Manila firm gave legal opinions on Philippine tax law to Philippine clients and signed them alone. Is he allowed to do so?

alac.answer: No; he is not allowed to practice Philippine law.
alac.basis: Under Rule 138 of the Rules of Court, only members of the Philippine Bar, who must be Filipino citizens, may practice law in the Philippines. A foreign lawyer not admitted here may act only within specific exceptions, such as representation in international arbitration under Section 22 of RA 9285, and even then may not appear as counsel in Philippine courts.
alac.application: Here, the American lawyer gave legal opinions on Philippine law to clients, which is the practice of law, though he is not a member of the Philippine Bar.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he is engaged in unauthorized practice, and the firm's Filipino partners who allow it may be disciplined.

keyPoints: Practice limited to members of the Philippine Bar
Foreign lawyers excluded except under specific laws
International arbitration exception (RA 9285, Sec. 22)
cite: Rule 138, Rules of Court; Alternative Dispute Resolution Act (RA 9285), Sec. 22

q: Among the privileges of a lawyer, when he appears for a client in court:
choices: He must always show a written power of attorney
He is presumed to be properly authorized to represent the client, and no written power of attorney is required
He may testify on any confidential matter
hints: The court may still require proof of authority on just cause.
Privileges come with duties.
why: Lawyers enjoy privileges such as the presumption of authority to appear for a client without a written power of attorney (subject to the court's power to require proof), the right to practice in all courts, privileged communication, and protection for statements made in pleadings relevant to the case.
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (formerly Rule 138, Sec. 21)

q: A lawyer entered his appearance for a defendant without attaching any written authority. The plaintiff moved to strike the appearance, arguing that a power of attorney is required. Rule on the motion.

alac.answer: The motion should be denied; the lawyer is presumed to be authorized.
alac.basis: A lawyer is presumed to be properly authorized to represent any cause in which he or she appears, and no written power of attorney is required to authorize him or her to appear in court for the client. However, the court may, on its own initiative or on motion of either party, on just cause, require the lawyer to produce or prove the authority under which he appears.
alac.application: Here, the plaintiff merely objects to the lack of a written authority, without showing any just cause to doubt the lawyer's authority.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the appearance stands, although the court may require proof of authority if just cause is shown later.

keyPoints: Presumption of authority to appear
No written power of attorney required
Court may require proof on just cause
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (formerly Rule 138, Sec. 21)

q: A non-lawyer who pretends to be a lawyer and appears in court may be punished for:
choices: Nothing, if he wins the case
Indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(e), among other liabilities
hints: Contempt is the usual penalty.
For Bar applicants, it may bar admission.
why: Unauthorized practice of law is punishable as indirect contempt (Rule 71, Sec. 3(e)); it may also bar admission to the Bar, lead to criminal liability (e.g., estafa or usurpation), and, for government lawyers who practice in violation of RA 6713, dismissal from service (Sec. 11).
cite: Rules of Court, Rule 71, Sec. 3(e); RA 6713, Sec. 11

q: Nilo, who never passed the Bar, used a lawyer's name and roll number, appeared in several hearings, and collected fees. What are the penalties he may face?

alac.answer: Nilo may be cited for indirect contempt and may face criminal liability.
alac.basis: Rule 71, Section 3(e) of the Rules of Court provides that a person guilty of assuming to be an attorney or an officer of a court, and acting as such without authority, may be punished for indirect contempt after charge and hearing. Using another person's name and collecting fees may also give rise to criminal liability, such as estafa or usurpation.
alac.application: Here, Nilo, a non-lawyer, assumed to be an attorney, appeared in hearings, and collected fees, using another lawyer's name and roll number.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he may be cited for indirect contempt and prosecuted for the crimes his acts constitute, and the lawyer whose name he used may be investigated if he consented.

keyPoints: Unauthorized practice punished as indirect contempt (Rule 71, Sec. 3(e))
Possible criminal liability
Liability of lawyers who abet
cite: Rules of Court, Rule 71, Sec. 3(e); RA 6713, Sec. 11

q: Under the CPRA, a lawyer may be disciplined for misconduct:
choices: Whether committed in his professional or private capacity, if it shows unfitness for the profession
Only if convicted of a crime
hints: Private misconduct may show unfitness.
The CPRA has six canons.
why: The CPRA applies to lawyers' conduct in and out of their profession; Canon II, Sec. 1 prohibits unlawful, dishonest, immoral or deceitful conduct, whether in professional or private capacity; the CPRA's general provisions set the canons (independence, propriety, fidelity, competence and diligence, equality, accountability).
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon II, Sec. 1

q: Atty. Ramos, in a private business deal unrelated to his practice, issued worthless checks to his suppliers and refused to pay. He argues that the CPRA covers only his conduct as a lawyer. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, he may be disciplined for his private misconduct.
alac.basis: Canon II, Section 1 of the CPRA provides that a lawyer shall not engage in unlawful, dishonest, immoral, or deceitful conduct. Conduct is not confined to the performance of a lawyer's professional duties; a lawyer may be disciplined for misconduct committed either in his professional or private capacity when it shows him unfit for the office and unworthy of the privileges of the profession.
alac.application: Here, Atty. Ramos issued worthless checks and refused to pay his debts, which is unlawful and dishonest conduct, even though it arose from a private business deal.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he may be disciplined under the CPRA.

keyPoints: CPRA covers professional and private conduct
Canon II, Sec. 1: no unlawful, dishonest, immoral or deceitful conduct
Issuing worthless checks shows unfitness
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon II, Sec. 1

q: Under Canon I (Independence) of the CPRA, a lawyer shall:
choices: Follow every instruction of the client
Make legal services accessible efficiently and effectively while maintaining independence and integrity
hints: Independence from clients, courts and others.
Lawyers decide procedure and strategy.
why: CPRA Canon I requires lawyers to maintain independence and integrity, be free from improper influences, and exercise their own judgment on procedure and strategy, while making legal services accessible.
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon I, Sec. 1

q: A client insisted that his lawyer file a groundless motion for the sole purpose of delaying the case, threatening to withdraw the engagement otherwise. What should the lawyer do?

alac.answer: The lawyer should refuse to file the groundless motion, even at the risk of losing the client.
alac.basis: Canon I, Section 1 of the CPRA provides that a lawyer shall make legal services accessible in an efficient and effective manner, and in performing this duty, a lawyer shall maintain independence, act with integrity, and at all times ensure the efficient and effective delivery of justice. The CPRA also gives the lawyer the discretion in matters of procedure and strategy, and prohibits delaying tactics.
alac.application: Here, the client wants a groundless motion filed solely to delay the case, which would defeat the efficient delivery of justice. The lawyer's independence requires him to exercise his own judgment, not blindly follow the client.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the lawyer should refuse and may withdraw from the engagement if the client insists.

keyPoints: Independence (Canon I, Sec. 1)
Efficient and effective delivery of justice
No dilatory motions
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon I, Sec. 1

q: Under the CPRA's rules on the responsible use of social media, a lawyer may NOT:
choices: Post legal information for the public
Knowingly or maliciously post false or unverified statements, or publish pleadings in a pending case to discredit the opposing party
hints: Online conduct is subject to the CPRA.
Privileged information must not be posted.
why: CPRA Canon II, Secs. 36-44 require responsible use of social media: no false or unverified posts, no fake accounts, no disclosure of privileged information, no use of social media to influence courts, and care in giving legal advice online. Lawyers have been disciplined for posting draft complaints to shame opponents (Lao v. Causing, A.C. No. 13453, October 4, 2022) and for viral profane videos (In re: Gadon, A.C. No. 13521, June 27, 2023).
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon II, Secs. 36-44; Lao v. Causing, A.C. No. 13453, October 4, 2022

q: Atty. Toni posted on Facebook a draft criminal complaint against a former mayor, with captions calling him a "thief," before the complaint was even filed. Is this proper?

alac.answer: No, it violates the CPRA's rules on social media and the sub judice and fairness rules.
alac.basis: Canon II, Section 38 of the CPRA provides that a lawyer shall not knowingly or maliciously post, share, upload or otherwise disseminate false or unverified statements, claims, or commit any other act of disinformation. In Lao v. Causing, A.C. No. 13453, October 4, 2022, the Supreme Court disciplined a lawyer who posted on Facebook a draft complaint, not yet filed, with insulting captions, holding that this was meant to shame and harass the respondent rather than seek justice.
alac.application: Here, Atty. Toni posted an unfiled complaint with captions branding the mayor a thief, which publicizes unverified accusations and uses social media to pressure and humiliate the other party.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Atty. Toni may be disciplined under the CPRA.

keyPoints: Responsible use of social media (Canon II, Secs. 36-44)
No false or unverified posts
Lao v. Causing
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon II, Secs. 36-44; Lao v. Causing, A.C. No. 13453, October 4, 2022

q: Under Canon III, Section 51 of the CPRA and Article 1491(5) of the Civil Code, a lawyer may NOT:
choices: Receive a fee after the case
Acquire a proprietary interest in the property or rights that are the object of a litigation in which he takes part
Buy property not involved in his cases
hints: The prohibition applies while the case is pending.
Contingent fees are allowed if reasonable.
why: CPRA Canon III, Sec. 51 (based on Civil Code Art. 1491(5)) prohibits lawyers from acquiring property or rights in litigation or transactions they handle; a contingent fee agreement payable after the case is not covered, as the transfer happens after the litigation ends.
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon III, Sec. 51; Civil Code, Art. 1491(5)

q: While a land case was pending, Atty. Uy accepted from his client a deed of sale over half of the disputed land as his fee. Is the transfer valid, and is he liable?

alac.answer: The transfer is void, and Atty. Uy may be disciplined.
alac.basis: Canon III, Section 51 of the CPRA provides that a lawyer shall not acquire, directly or indirectly, a proprietary interest in the property or rights which is the object of any litigation or transaction in which the lawyer may take part by virtue of the profession. Article 1491(5) of the Civil Code likewise prohibits lawyers from acquiring by purchase property and rights in litigation in which they take part.
alac.application: Here, Atty. Uy acquired half of the disputed land while the case he was handling was pending. That is exactly what the law prohibits; it is different from a contingent fee payable after the case ends.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale is void, and Atty. Uy is liable for violating the CPRA.

keyPoints: No acquisition of property in litigation (Canon III, Sec. 51)
Civil Code Art. 1491(5)
Contingent fee after judgment is different
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon III, Sec. 51; Civil Code, Art. 1491(5)

q: Under Canon V, Section 3 of the CPRA, a lawyer may refuse to represent an indigent person only if:
choices: He cannot carry out the work effectively or competently for justifiable cause, he would be placed in a conflict of interest, or he is related to the adverse party within the prohibited degree
hints: Inability to pay is not a ground.
The exceptions are limited.
why: CPRA Canon V, Sec. 3 bars refusing an indigent client except for justifiable inability, conflict of interest, or relationship with the adverse party; legal aid is a duty supported by the ULAS rules (AM 22-11-01-SC).
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon V, Sec. 3; Unified Legal Aid Service Rules (AM 22-11-01-SC)

q: An indigent farmer asked Atty. Vale to represent him in a land case. Atty. Vale declined, saying the case would not pay and he was busy with paying clients. Is his refusal proper?

alac.answer: No, his refusal is not proper.
alac.basis: Canon V, Section 3 of the CPRA provides that a lawyer shall not refuse the representation of an indigent person, except if the lawyer is not in a position to carry out the work effectively or competently due to a justifiable cause, the lawyer will be placed in a conflict-of-interest situation, or the lawyer is related to the potential adverse party within the prohibited degree.
alac.application: Here, Atty. Vale refused because the case would not pay and he preferred paying clients. Neither reason is among the exceptions; being busy with paying clients is not a justifiable cause for inability.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, his refusal violates the CPRA.

keyPoints: No refusal of indigent clients (Canon V, Sec. 3)
Limited exceptions
Legal aid as a duty (ULAS)
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon V, Sec. 3; Unified Legal Aid Service Rules (AM 22-11-01-SC)

q: Under Canon IV of the CPRA, a lawyer who fails to file an appeal brief, causing the dismissal of the client's appeal, violates:
choices: No rule, since the client should follow up
The duty of competence and diligence
hints: The client's follow-up is not required.
Failure to update the client is also a violation.
why: CPRA Canon IV, Sec. 1 requires competent, efficient and conscientious service; Sec. 3 requires diligent and seasonable action and punctuality; Sec. 6 requires updating the client; neglect of a legal matter is a ground for discipline.
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon IV, Secs. 1 and 3

q: Atty. Wenceslao received the notice to file an appeal brief but forgot to file it. The appeal was dismissed, and he did not tell the client for months. What did he violate?

alac.answer: He violated the duties of competence and diligence and the duty to update the client.
alac.basis: Canon IV, Section 3 of the CPRA provides that a lawyer shall diligently and seasonably act on any legal matter entrusted by a client, and Section 6 requires the lawyer to update the client on the status of the case. Section 1 requires legal service that is competent, efficient, and conscientious.
alac.application: Here, Atty. Wenceslao failed to file the appeal brief, causing the dismissal of the appeal, and did not inform the client for months.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he may be suspended from the practice of law, the penalty depending on the damage and circumstances.

keyPoints: Competence (Canon IV, Sec. 1)
Diligence and punctuality (Sec. 3)
Duty to update the client (Sec. 6)
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon IV, Secs. 1 and 3

q: Under Canon V, Section 1 of the CPRA, a lawyer may NOT decline to represent a person solely because of:
choices: The person's ethnicity, sexual orientation or gender identity, religion, disability, or the public's opinion of his guilt
The lawyer's lack of competence in the field
hints: Public opinion of guilt is not a valid reason.
The standard of service must be equal.
why: CPRA Canon V (Equality) prohibits declining representation on discriminatory grounds and requires special care for vulnerable persons (Sec. 2) and indigent persons (Sec. 3), with the same standard of service for all (Sec. 4).
cite: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA, AM 22-09-01-SC), Canon V, Sec. 1
